title: Rehat and joy
hookLine: discipline as a frame for a joyful life

lines: JOY HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.
A CODE OF DISCIPLINES, A SONG OF JOY.
cards: Joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the opening of the Anand Sahib, a hymn by Guru Amar Das, in paraphrase, and you met it early on this path. Anand means joy, bliss.
Sikhs sing it in the evening prayers, its verses are sung as ceremonies close, and the Sikh wedding takes its name from the same word: Anand Karaj, the ceremony of joy.
Yet the code is full of disciplines: rise early, cover the hair, refuse the drink, keep the promise. How do the two go together?

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.
teach.b: Start with how the Guru Granth Sahib itself is built. The heart of it is arranged by raag, a musical measure.
Each raag has its own rules: which notes belong, which are left out, the mood it carries, often the time of day it suits. A musician who ignores those rules doesn't get more freedom; they get noise.
A musician who keeps them gets music. So the scripture holds its song inside a discipline.
Back to the Anand Sahib. Guru Amar Das doesn't say joy came by escaping anything. In paraphrase, it came by finding the Guru, and with it, the hymn says, the raags themselves came to sing the Word.
The joy has a source and a shape.

Then there's chardi kala, rising spirits, an outlook that keeps lifting. It's in the Ardas, near the end: with the Name, may spirits rise. Sikh tradition holds it up in hard times too; it isn't a mood for easy days only.
Set this beside the code. The morning banis frame the day the way a raag frames a song. The kesh, the kara, the clear mind, faithfulness at home, honest work: they're the notes the life is played in.
Inside that frame there's room for a lot of joy. A langar hall can be loud with talk and laughter. Hola Mohalla has horses and games.
A wedding goes around the Granth to singing. The discipline isn't the opposite of the joy.

teach.h: THE FRAME GIVES JOY A PLACE TO LIVE.
teach.b: It's what gives the joy somewhere to live.

how: Sikhs sing the Anand Sahib in the evening Rehras and as ceremonies close, the wedding is called the Anand Karaj, and the Ardas asks for chardi kala, rising spirits.

o: a festival day when the code's rules are paused
discipline as the frame that gives joy a home
giving up joy in order to keep the discipline

games.q: inside rehat and joy: tap the pairs.
p: a musical measure with its own rules

s: a strict code leaves no room for joy
Sikh life keeps naming joy: the Anand Sahib, the Anand Karaj, chardi kala in the Ardas.
the heart of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raag
each raag has its own notes and mood. the scripture itself is joy held inside a discipline.
in the Anand Sahib, joy comes from escaping every rule
Guru Amar Das says joy came by finding the true Guru.

games.q: a musician wants more freedom, so she ignores the raag's rules and plays any note she likes. what happens?
o: she gets noise, not the raag.
games.why: a raag's rules are what make it that raag. the frame gives the music somewhere to live, the way rehat frames a joyful life.

practice: Pick one thing you do on purpose, regularly: a walk, a prayer, a song you practice, a meal you cook the same way. Do a tiny bit of it slowly now if you can, or bring it to mind in detail.
Look for the small gladness inside the routine, the first step, the warm pan, the note landing right, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Rehat and joy. In Sikh life discipline is a frame for joy, the way a raag frames a song. The Anand Sahib opens with joy that has come, and the Ardas asks for rising spirits. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: joy, bliss; the name of Guru Amar Das's hymn and of the Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj.

carryVoice: Your line: discipline and joy. The frame and the song belong together. Thirteen hundred days, and still climbing.
